newsitem.title: HONG KONG: YEAR-Asia's local bond markets make strides in '96.
newsitem.headline: YEAR-Asia's local bond markets make strides in '96.

text.p: Asia's local currency bond markets made major strides in 1996 as issuers and investors found their needs converging, analysts said.

"This year has seen tremendous new investor interest as well as a number of Asian companies issuing in local currencies," said Rosa Wang, senior portfolio manager at Peregrine Fixed Income in Hong Kong.

The need for infrastructure funding was widely touted as the impetus behind development of Asian bond markets, with the World Bank estimating the region's infrastructure requirements at about US$850 billion in the next five years.
But corporate funding needs were also key, experts said.
"I think that broadly based investment is going to be many multiples of the numbers we keep talking about in terms of infrastructure," World Bank managing director Gautam Kaji said.

There was a growing demand for longer-term financing by Asian companies, he said. That reflected a change in the region's industrial base from export firms requiring short-term funding to manufacturers looking further ahead.
"The industrial map is changing which requires much more longer-term fixed asset creation which cannot be funded just by commercial banks and self-financed equity," he said.
Peregrine's Wang said that while infrastructure needs would likely drive bond market development over the next decade, corporations had been the main force recently.
"In this past year and really for the last few years, we have not seen much which is directly infrastructure related or project finance related," said Wang.
"What we have seen is that it is either banks that finance companies in Asia or the corporations themselves that are borrowing," she said.
CORPORARE BOND MARKETS GROW FASTER
Because many Asian countries run fiscal surpluses and have no reason to borrow, corporate bond markets in the region have grown faster than the government bond markets.

While vibrant corporate markets can be created even in the absence of an active government market, analysts said government bond markets could provide important market infrastructure such benchmarks and liquidity.
A few Asian countries had made significant progress in extending yield curves this year, analysts said.

"In a lot of places the basic market infrastructure that makes conventional markets possible is starting to happen in terms of the creation of decent benchmark curves and in government markets starting to function effectively," said Kenneth Yeadon, head of Asia fixed income at HSBC Markets.
Hong Kong maintains its place as Asia's most advanced government bond market, bankers said.

In addition to extending the yield curve with the introduction of a 10-year note, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority gave the go-ahead for the establishment of a mortgage corporation along the lines of the U.S. agency Fannie Mae and has introduced refinements to its securities settlement.
The Philippines also introduced a 10-year bond this year that was warmly received by investors.

"Some of the new boys on the block like the Philippines have actually made some of the biggest progress in getting a benchmark yield curve going," said Imre Speizer, director of local fixed income trading at SBC Warburg in Singpore.
"I would say that outside of Hong Kong dollar bonds, the Philippines probably has the best available yield curve of all the ASEAN countries," he said.
Other countries also are looking to establish longer-dated benchmarks and build up market infrastructure.
Malaysia, for example, may introduce a zero coupon bond, while Indonesia had been working with the International Finance Corp to establish a local-currency benchmark, bankers said.
Market liberalisation, tax reform, improved regulatory systems and better clearing mechanisms are routinely cited as necessary for the advancement of Asia's bond markets.
DRIVING THE MARKETS
But market watchers said supply/demand fundamentals were driving the markets along, even though governments made little progress in those areas in 1996.

"There hasn't been anything drastic that has occurred in terms of infrastructure in Thailand or Indonesia this year, for example, but there are things that have to be developed organically," said Speizer.

For example, turnover in Indonesia is almost as high as in Thailand, particularly in the short end. Last year, Indonesia's turnover was just 15-20 percent of Thailand's level and the change "is just a market thing", said Speizer.

HSBC's Yeadon noted that as Asian economies matured there was a convergence of issuer and investor needs. Pension funds that are taking root in the region need long-term assets to match liabilities and increasingly affluent Asians can provide the savings to invest in long-dated instruments.
Banks continue to be the major investors in Asian debt instruments as they try to expand from traditional lending into capital markets in order to fill their books, analysts said.

"A lot of international banks are setting up in Asia and since they don't have a track record it is hard for them to set up a lending operation so they get involved in debt securities to fill up their books," said a Singapore-based trading manager.
But institutional investors such as insurance and pension funds, mutual fund managers and private investors from both Asia and elsewhere were also getting involved, analysts said.
STRUCTURED MARKETS

In the more restricted bond markets, such as South Korea and India, fund managers report that investors are increasingly taking part by buying structured products that are tied to the performance of the bonds but are not directly exposed.
"We're certainly seeing a lot of that being done, but I think it is a temporary measure until markets open," said Wang.
Asian markets were becoming more open to foreign participation, but most governments prefered to take a gradual approach to minimise disruption to monetary planning, she said.
Because of their relative openness and high yields, the bond markets of Thailand and Indonesia are favorites among investors, though the Philippines is becoming more popular.
"I would say that Indonesia will definitely be the hot market of 1997. 1996 was Thailand's year, next year will be Indonesia's," predicted SBC's Speizer.
Some of the best developed markets, such as those in Malaysia and Hong Kong, were less enticing because they did not offer large yield pick-ups, fund managers said.
They said the outlook for 1997 would depend significantly on the direction of U.S. interest rates, since many Asian currencies are pegged to the U.S. dollar.
